messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Violence: Violence
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samuel is a 20-year-old African American man who came for treatment after months of feeling as if he were living inside a permanent state of alert. He is single and works as a doctor, a role he had once regarded as proof of who he was: disciplined, useful, and able to remain steady in crisis. During his combat deployment, that sense of himself was shaken in a way he has not been able to put back together. When he speaks about what happened, the account does not come smoothly. It arrives in abrupt fragments, and just as the memory begins to approach something more complete, he pulls away from it, looks down, and says he cannot go further.

What he can describe is enough to convey why certain moments now seize him so completely. He remembers being in a combat zone where violence had become ordinary right up until the instant it became immediate. There had been the tense expectation of danger, then a stretch of unnatural silence that felt wrong to him even then, as if everything had gone still just before something terrible broke through. After that, his recollection splinters. He can bring up disconnected images of violent injury, bodies moving and dropping, and the sense of air suddenly becoming hard to get. He remembers trying to breathe and feeling as if his chest would not work properly, but the sequence around that is missing. There are stretches he says are simply absent: no matter how hard he tries, he cannot recover them. The parts he does have do not fit neatly together, and this troubles him. He is left with isolated pieces—the silence, the violence, the struggle for breath—without a whole story he can hold in his mind.

In the weeks after he returned, he expected the intensity to wear off. Instead, ordinary moments began to take on the same quality as those fragments. If a room suddenly fell completely silent, Samuel would feel his body tense before he had fully registered what had happened around him. Silence did not feel peaceful; it felt like the split second before disaster. Encounters with violence, even when they were not directed at him—a heated altercation in public, footage on a waiting room television, a patient arriving after an assault—could abruptly narrow his attention until he was no longer fully in the present. Most unsettling of all was any moment of breathlessness. Climbing stairs too quickly at the hospital, wearing a mask through a long shift, or hurrying between patients and noticing he was short of breath could trigger a spike of fear that felt disproportionate even to him. In those moments he was certain he had to get control immediately.

At work, these reactions have become woven into his days. Hospital life contains the very things that now unsettle him: long stretches of hushed corridors, sudden eruptions of interpersonal violence in the emergency setting, and constant bodily awareness under pressure. Samuel has found himself avoiding parts of his own experience rather than only avoiding situations. When something at work stirs the memory, he pushes it away fast, almost reflexively, before the image can become fully clear. He has become skilled at cutting off recollection midstream, but he is also disturbed by how little access he has to the event as a whole. He worries about what it means that he cannot remember key parts and that when he tries, all he gets are broken pieces.

Over time, what has changed most is the way he thinks about himself and the world. He says he no longer knows who he is. Before combat, he believed there was a logic to effort and decency, that competence mattered, that the world could be dangerous but still basically made sense. Now he speaks as if those beliefs have been demolished. He has come to feel that danger can emerge without warning and that the only reasonable stance is constant readiness. He scans rooms automatically, notices shifts in noise, and remains on guard in a way that leaves little room for rest. He does not describe this as excessive; from his perspective it feels necessary. Letting down his guard seems irresponsible, almost naive.

Being single has meant that much of this has unfolded in private. He has continued functioning outwardly, especially at work, but with increasing strain. What brought him to seek help was not a single collapse so much as the accumulation of these moments: another episode at the hospital when he noticed himself short of breath and had to step away, another instant when sudden silence made his whole body brace, another realization that he could not tell a coherent story about the event that changed him. He came in afraid that the person he was before is gone for good, and hoping, more tentatively, that he might still find some way to live without feeling under threat every minute.
